blunt_right: No notice by text is common in kitchens; restaurant turnover runs 70-100%+ annually and a cook leaving for a nearby opener is a routine pattern, not a personal verdict on you. Legally: absent a signed contract requiring notice, he owed you none -- at-will employment cuts both ways. A non-compete against a line cook is generally unenforceable in most states even where one exists; do not threaten legal action over it, and do not badmouth him to suppliers or the new employer -- that risks a defamation claim against you. Pay his final wages and any accrued, legally-owed leave promptly regardless of how he left; getting that wrong creates liability on top of a bad week. Staffing, today: contact a staffing agency or post on Culinary Agents and local industry groups for an interim cook; cross-train your strongest prep or serving staff on a reduced menu to cut the labor load now; shrink the menu temporarily rather than running 15-hour days indefinitely, which degrades your judgment and food-safety compliance and puts you at risk of the same burnout-driven exit. Consider why he left: pay, hours, proximity, and advancement are the four most common reasons cooks jump even after good treatment -- if you can ask him directly, without confrontation, the answer tells you what to fix before the next hire leaves the same way. Build redundancy now: cross-train two people on every station so one resignation can't take down service again. What you did for him when his daughter was hospitalized was the right call regardless of what he did afterward; it did not create an obligation on his part, and his leaving does not retroactively make it worthless.

blunt_right: Condensation and penetrating or rising damp look different and require different fixes; the agent's stock answer assumes the former without inspection, which is not evidence, it's deflection. Structure the email around obligation, not description. State: the exact dates of your four prior emails; that the disrepair has now persisted three months; and that under landlord repairing obligations (Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.11, and the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018 if this is England), damp affecting a structural wall may be a category 1 or 2 hazard under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System, which the landlord is required to investigate rather than assume a cause for. Request a professional damp survey in writing, with a fixed deadline -- ten working days is standard. State explicitly that if no inspection is arranged by that date, you will report the property to the local council's Environmental Health team, who can compel inspection and repair under the Housing Act 2004. Attach dated photos or video, and a hygrometer reading if you have one, showing humidity levels inconsistent with simple condensation. Do not withhold rent -- it risks eviction proceedings unless done through a formal repair-and-deduct process most tenancies don't support. Check your tenancy paperwork for a redress scheme membership (Property Redress Scheme or The Property Ombudsman) and name it, stating you will escalate there next. Keep all correspondence in writing, not calls, for the record. If other flats in the building have reported similar damp, say so -- that points to a structural cause rather than your behavior, and changes how the agent has to respond.
